# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
This comment does two different things. Sections 1–5 are a careful, data-based correction of the Halden pilot, and most of it holds up. Sections 6–8, the abstract and the conclusion then make a much stronger claim, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact," which the comment's own numbers and the Varden trial it cites do not support. Most important first:

## 1. The headline conclusion contradicts the comment's own evidence

The conclusion says the per-hour gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty." Two things stand against that:

- **The comment's own corrections leave a gain.** After fixing output and hours, it finds +10.8%. Removing that residual relies entirely on the novelty argument in Section 6, which is a hypothesis, not a measurement (see point 4).
- **It cites the Varden trial selectively.** Varden's case-processing stratum used record-based output, actual hours from timesheets and a randomised control group. That design addresses all three of the comment's measurement and selection problems, and it still found +12.5% output per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4). Even Varden's counter stratum, which the comment calls "the most reliable finding in the literature," showed +6.7% per actual hour. The comment cites the output loss from that stratum and omits the per-hour gain from the same table, and it never mentions the case-processing result.

Section 6 says "the burden of proof lies with those claiming" a durable effect. "Entirely an artifact" is also a positive claim and needs evidence too. The data note concedes that the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole," which is incompatible with a conclusion about reduced-hours schemes in general. A defensible conclusion would be: the Halden figure is overstated by more than half; a gain of roughly 10% remains in the subset that can be checked; whether it lasts is unknown.

## 2. The abstract misstates what was corrected

The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems (attrition, output and hours) reduces the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects **only output and hours**. Attrition is not corrected anywhere. The nine withdrawn organisations are absent from every row.

Since attrition probably biases the result upward, a fully corrected figure might be lower. But the comment shouldn't say it has made a correction it hasn't. It could bound the effect instead: assign the seven post-start withdrawals a range of plausible outcomes, or use whatever output data exist for their months in the pilot.

## 3. The hours breakdown doesn't add up

Section 3 attributes the gap between the 20% scheduled cut and the 14.1% actual cut to two sources:

- +0.7 hours per day on four days, i.e. 2.8 hours a week; and
- 1.6 hours a week logged on the day off.

Those total 4.4 extra hours. On a 32-hour schedule that implies about 36.4 hours, or 36.6 if the +0.7 is measured against baseline day length (40.3 / 5 ≈ 8.06 hours). The reported pilot average is **34.6**. The components overstate the total by roughly 2 hours, and the authors should reconcile this.

The main figures themselves check out: 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859, and every row of Table 2 matches.

## 4. The novelty argument is thin and leaves the obvious test undone

- **Energy is not output.** The argument rests on self-reported energy declining, then assumes output per hour will follow. But Halden collected the output index **monthly**, and the comment has the microdata. If novelty drives the gain, output per hour should rise early and fall back by month six. That is a direct test, and it isn't reported.
- **The extrapolation is weak.** It is a straight line through two points after an initial rise. There is no reason to assume a linear decline rather than a plateau. Even on its own terms, the decline of 0.32 SD per three months reaches zero around month 8.7, not "around month ten."
- **Varden weighs against it.** The comment's novelty setting is "a change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation." Varden staff didn't choose: offices were randomly assigned. The per-hour gain was still present at nine months, longer than the Halden pilot ran. Nine months is too short to settle the question, but it is evidence, and the comment doesn't engage with it.

## 5. Section 7 mischaracterises the Varden meetings analysis

The comment says the Varden authors "suggest this as a mechanism" and that it "should not be cited as a mechanism." The Varden paper says that a correlation across seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," labels the analysis unregistered and exploratory, and has registered a confirmatory test. Their framing is essentially the comment's.

Two specific claims are also inaccurate:

- **"Fitted to a subgroup."** The seven offices are all of the treated case-processing offices, not a chosen subset.
- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known."** The calendar data were collected in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed. What was post hoc was the decision to analyse them, which Varden discloses.

There are fair criticisms the comment could make. The correlation is not significant (r = 0.71 with n = 7 gives p ≈ 0.07). And as I noted on the Varden paper, there are no baseline meeting data, so "offices that cut meetings most" can't actually be measured. Either point would be a stronger critique than the one made.

## 6. The record-based output measure has its own bias

Section 2 treats records as the true measure and manager ratings as inflated. That is probably right on average; 19 of 23 managers rated higher than their records. But one of the record types listed is **"billable hours delivered."** That is closer to an input than an output, and it falls mechanically when hours are cut. Organisations using it will show an output loss whatever happened to productivity, which biases the record-based index down.

The comment should report the manager-versus-record gap by record type, or drop billable-hours organisations as a check. It should also note that some manager ratings may legitimately reflect output the records miss.

## 7. Section-level points

- **Attrition (§1)** is the comment's most important new finding. The working paper said withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata say seven of nine withdrew after the schedule started, and six of nine cited workload. If confirmed, that is a material misreport, and the Halden authors should be invited to respond.
- **Revenue (§4):** the deflation is correct (1.014 / 1.041 ≈ 0.974, so −2.6%). Two caveats: CPI is a crude deflator for organisations' own output prices, and a real decline without a control group shows only that the nominal figure was misleading, not that the pilot caused the fall. The comment's wording ("misleading impression") is appropriately limited.
- **Retail (§5):** the −11.2% comes from **three organisations**, and setting it beside Varden's −11.4% compares an uncontrolled before-and-after with a difference-in-differences estimate. The similarity is suggestive, not confirmation. The point that the per-hour metric guarantees "gains in every sector" is correct and well made.
- **Weighting:** Halden reported employee-weighted means. The comment doesn't say whether its subset figures are weighted the same way. If not, the rows of Table 2 aren't strictly comparable.
- **Recommendations (§8)** are sound, especially analysing all enrolled organisations, including those that withdraw.

## Overall

As a correction of the Halden pilot, this is valuable. The attrition finding, the manager-versus-records gap and the actual-hours correction are all well documented. They justify cutting the headline from 23.4% to roughly 11% and suspecting that attrition makes even that too high. The comment goes wrong when it turns "overstated, and possibly temporary" into "entirely an artifact." That step depends on an untested novelty hypothesis and on leaving out the randomised evidence that cuts against it.

The comment would be stronger if it:

- dropped "entirely";
- reported the monthly output trajectory as a direct test of novelty;
- engaged with Varden's case-processing result;
- fixed the abstract and the hours arithmetic.
